# Upgrade a self-hosted install

An upgrade replaces the app, worker and web containers. Your documents and settings stay in the database and the file store, so they are not touched. The database moves forward by itself: every start applies the migrations it has not had yet, before the app begins to answer.

## Before you upgrade

1. **Take a backup** of the database, the file store and the `appdata` volume. The steps are in [Back up and restore](/docs/self-host-backup). Do this every time; it is the only way back.
2. Read the [changelog](/changelog) for the versions between yours and the new one.
3. Check that nobody is in the middle of signing. A signing session in progress survives an upgrade, but the page reloads once.

## Upgrade

```bash
git pull
docker compose build
docker compose up -d
```

`up -d` recreates only the containers whose image changed. The database and the converter keep running. The file store's image is built here too, so it restarts when it was rebuilt; for about twenty seconds after that, `/readyz` answers `not_ready` with `storage` failing, then `ready`.

Then delete the old images, which take several gigabytes and are no longer used:

```bash
docker image prune -f
```

## Check that it worked

```bash
docker compose ps
docker compose exec -T app node -e "fetch('http://localhost:8080/readyz').then(r=>r.text()).then(console.log)"
```

The app's own `/readyz` check (it is not reachable from outside, which is intended) lists the number of migrations applied. It answers `"status":"ready"` once the database, the file store and the signing certificate are all reachable. Then open the app, send yourself a test document and sign it.

## If something looks wrong

Look at the logs first:

```bash
docker compose logs --tail 100 app worker
```

A migration that cannot apply stops the new app from starting, and the log says which one. Do not keep retrying: restore the backup you took (see [Back up and restore](/docs/self-host-backup)), go back to the version you had, and report the log.

```bash
git checkout <the version you had>
docker compose build && docker compose up -d
```

Migrations are written to only add things, but the supported way back is the backup, not running an older version on a newer database.

## The built-in templates

The 54 built-in templates (24 Document, 30 Form) are seeded by the worker: on install it prints every one for each workspace, and on an upgrade that changes a template it makes a new version of that template's read-only master, so a form or an automation that uses it follows. Nothing you customized is touched, and nothing here counts toward any limit. The worker logs `seed_template_library` with how many masters it printed.

## Keep your secrets

Never delete `.env` or the `appdata` volume during an upgrade. The first holds the secrets that protect sign-in tokens; the second holds the certificate that seals your signed PDFs and the key that protects stored passwords.


---

# Back up and restore

A self-hosted Docustay keeps its state in three places. Back up all three, together, or the backup may not restore.

| What | Where | Why it matters |
|---|---|---|
| The database | the `db` container (volume `dbdata`) | People, templates, documents, settings, the audit trail. |
| The file store | the `storage` container (volume `filedata`) | Uploaded files and signed PDFs, each sealed with its workspace's own key (see below). |
| The app data volume and `.env` | volume `appdata` and the file `docustay/.env` | The certificate that seals signed PDFs, the key that protects stored passwords, and the secrets behind sign-in. Without them a restored copy cannot open what it stored. |

## Back up

Run this from the `docustay` folder. It writes one dated folder.

```bash
set -eu
d="backup-$(date +%Y%m%d-%H%M)"; mkdir -p "$d"
# 1. the database, as one consistent file
docker compose exec -T db pg_dump -U docustay -Fc docustay > "$d/db.dump"
# 2. the file store and the app data volume, as archives
# the volumes are named after the Compose project (docustay_filedata for a standard install); a wrong name would silently back up an empty volume, so ask the running database container which project it belongs to, then check the volumes exist
pj=$(docker inspect "$(docker compose ps -q db)" --format '{{ index .Config.Labels "com.docker.compose.project" }}')
for v in filedata appdata; do
  docker volume inspect "${pj}_$v" >/dev/null || { echo "no volume ${pj}_$v: run this from the install folder" >&2; exit 1; }
  docker run --rm -v "${pj}_$v:/v:ro" -v "$PWD/$d:/out" alpine tar czf "/out/$v.tgz" -C /v .
done
# 3. the settings file
cp .env "$d/env"; chmod 600 "$d/env"
# 4. check the folder is whole: every file exists and is not empty
for f in db.dump filedata.tgz appdata.tgz env; do
  [ -s "$d/$f" ] || { echo "BACKUP INCOMPLETE: $d/$f is missing or empty" >&2; exit 1; }
done
ls -l "$d"
echo "backed up to $d"
```

Copy the folder somewhere that is not this machine. The folder holds secrets, so keep it as private as the install itself.

## Restore on a new machine

The database dump holds the tables but not the database's logins (the roles the app and the worker connect as). Those are created the first time the install starts, so a restore starts the install once on an empty database first. Restoring into a database that has no roles leaves the worker without access to its own tables and the install crash-loops with "permission denied for schema graphile_worker".

1. Install Docker and get the Docustay folder (`git clone`, then `cd docustay`).
2. Put the saved settings file back: `cp backup-…/env .env`
3. Start the install once on its empty database so it creates its roles and tables, and wait until `app` says `(healthy)`:

```bash
docker compose up -d
docker compose ps
```

4. Stop everything that writes, and the file store as well, keeping only the database running (the file store reads its files when it starts, so if it keeps running while its volume is replaced it carries on serving the empty volume it had, and every signed copy answers 502):

```bash
docker compose stop app worker web storage
```

5. Empty the database of what the first start created, then load the dump. The first start made the tables of the version you have checked out, and an older backup does not contain every one of them, so loading over them with `--clean` is refused ("cannot drop … because other objects depend on it"). Dropping the five application schemas first works for a backup from any older version, and the install brings the restored database up to date the next time it starts:

```bash
docker compose exec -T db psql -U docustay -d docustay -v ON_ERROR_STOP=1 -c "DROP SCHEMA IF EXISTS keystone, keystone_auth, keystone_meta, graphile_worker, stripe CASCADE; DROP FUNCTION IF EXISTS public.set_updated_at() CASCADE;"
docker compose exec -T db pg_restore -U docustay -d docustay < backup-…/db.dump
```

`pg_restore` should print nothing and finish without an error. If it prints errors, stop and do not go on to step 6.

6. Load the two volumes:

```bash
pj=$(docker inspect "$(docker compose ps -q db)" --format '{{ index .Config.Labels "com.docker.compose.project" }}')
for v in filedata appdata; do
  docker run --rm -v "${pj}_$v:/v" -v "$PWD/backup-…:/in:ro" alpine sh -c "cd /v && tar xzf /in/$v.tgz"
done
```

7. Start everything, the file store included, and check it: `docker compose up -d`, then run `docker compose ps` and open the app. Every service should be `Up`, and `app` should say `(healthy)`. The app's own `/readyz` check (see [Upgrade](/docs/self-host-upgrade.md)) says `not_ready` for about ten seconds while the file store loads its files, then `ready`; it lists the migrations applied, which will be more than the old install's if you restored an older backup, because the start brings the database up to date.

## Your files are sealed: what that means for a backup

Docustay encrypts every file it stores (uploads, signed copies, certificates, printed templates) before it reaches the file store, with a data key that belongs to the workspace alone. The data key is kept in the database, sealed under `KEYSTONE_MASTER_KEY` from your `.env`. So a file opens only when **all three** are present: the file store, the database, and the `.env` key.

- A copy of the file store without the database cannot be opened. A database without the file store has no files. A restored database and file store with a **different** `KEYSTONE_MASTER_KEY` cannot be opened either, so keep the `.env` backup, apart from the others, as carefully as the key itself.
- Take the database dump and the file-store archive at the same time (the backup script above does). A workspace key is never deleted while the workspace exists, so a dump taken after a file was stored always holds the key that opens it; a dump older than a key rotation does not hold the newer key, and files moved onto it afterwards will not open from that older dump.
- After a restore, check that the files open. This reads up to 20 stored files for one workspace and prints whether each opens; it changes nothing:

```bash
docker compose exec app node docustay/entrypoint.mjs run scripts/file-keys.mjs verify <workspace id>
```

`status` lists every workspace's keys. `rotate <workspace id>` makes a new key active and moves that workspace's files onto it; `seal` runs the same pass the worker runs at every start (it seals any file stored before encryption was switched on, and does nothing when there is nothing to do). Once every workspace shows "all files sealed", you can set `DOCUSTAY_REFUSE_PLAINTEXT_FILES=on` in `.env` so a file in the store that is not sealed is refused instead of served.

## After a restore: carry out the deletions again

A restore rewinds the database, so a person or a workspace that was deleted after the backup was taken comes back with it. Every deletion Docustay carries out leaves one small entry in a deletion ledger in the file store (under `_platform_ledger/deletion/`): a SHA-256 of the lower-cased email address or the workspace id, the date and a request id, never a name. After the restore, and once the install is up again, run the replay script. The first command only lists what would be deleted again; the second does it:

```bash
docker compose exec app node docustay/entrypoint.mjs run scripts/replay-deletions.mjs
docker compose exec app node docustay/entrypoint.mjs run scripts/replay-deletions.mjs --apply
```

It is safe to run twice: whatever is already gone is skipped. The ledger lives in the file store, so it only holds deletions the file store you are using has seen. If you also restore the file store from the same backup, deletions made after that backup are not in the ledger and cannot be replayed; in that case, if you know whose details were deleted, delete them again by hand.

## Test the restore

A backup you have not restored is a guess. Once, on a spare machine, do the restore above and open a signed document. Do it again after a major upgrade.

## How often

Daily is a good start for the database. The file store changes only when documents are made or signed, so the same schedule is enough. Keep at least the last seven.


---

# Harden a self-hosted install

Run Docustay on your own servers and you choose every provider that touches your documents. This page is the checklist for an install that holds sensitive documents. Work through it top to bottom after [installing](/self-host) and before the first real document.

Docustay is not for protected health information yet, on our hosted service or on your own servers. This page is not legal advice.

## 1. Set the workspace's security settings

In **Workspace → Security**, an owner or admin can set these for everyone in the workspace:

| What | Setting |
|---|---|
| Two-step sign-in | Offered to everyone. Tick **Require two-step sign-in for every team member** to make it required; set it up for yourself first |
| Idle sign-out | Off by default. Choose 15, 30 or 60 minutes, or 4 or 8 hours |
| Access log | Always on: every view, download and export by your team, with a CSV |
| Signed copies | Attached to the email by default; Settings → Download links can send a link instead |

## 2. Keep the inside private

- **Only the web container listens.** In the bundled `docker-compose.yml` only `web` publishes a port. The database, the file store and the PDF converter talk on Compose's private network. Do not add `ports:` to `db`, `storage` or `gotenberg`.
- **Put HTTPS in front.** Use a reverse proxy with TLS ([reverse proxy guide](/docs/self-host-reverse-proxy)). Set `KEYSTONE_PUBLIC_URL` to the `https://` address and `KEYSTONE_TRUSTED_PROXY_HOPS` to the number of proxies in front. Docustay sends HSTS on every HTTPS answer.
- **Firewall the host.** Allow 443 (and 80 for the certificate check) in; nothing else from outside.

## 3. Encrypt what is stored

- **Disks.** Put the Docker volumes (`dbdata`, `filedata`, `appdata`) on an encrypted disk: LUKS on Linux, or your cloud provider's encrypted volumes.
- **Secrets and files.** `init.sh` writes `KEYSTONE_MASTER_KEY`, which seals stored secrets (two-step secrets, SMTP passwords, webhook secrets) and each workspace's file key; every stored document file is encrypted under its workspace's own key (see [Back up and restore](/docs/self-host-backup)). The database and the disks are not encrypted by Docustay, so the disk advice above still applies. Keep `.env` readable only by the account that runs Docker (`chmod 600 .env`).
- **Backups.** Encrypt each backup before it leaves the machine (for example `age` or `gpg`), and keep the key apart from the backup. See [Back up and restore](/docs/self-host-backup).

```bash
# encrypt last night's backup folder for one recipient key, then copy only the .age file off the machine
d=$(ls -d backup-* | tail -1)
tar czf - "$d" | age -r "$(cat ~/.docustay-backup.pub)" > "$d.tgz.age"
```

## 4. Choose your providers

Everything that sends, stores or reads your documents is a provider you choose.

- **Email.** Set `RESEND_API_KEY`, or use your own SMTP server in Settings → Email.
- **Sign-in.** The built-in sign-in (`KEYSTONE_LOCAL_AUTH`) keeps identities in your own database. Or connect your own OpenID Connect provider (`DOCUSTAY_OIDC_ISSUER`, see [single sign-on](/docs/self-host-sso)).
- **AI.** Leave `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` empty if documents must not leave your servers for drafting.
- **Hosting.** Your server or cloud provider holds the disks.

## 5. Sign-in and sessions

- Two-step sign-in is offered to everyone; an owner can require it for the whole team.
- Turn on passkeys (`KEYSTONE_PASSKEYS=1` and `KEYSTONE_PASSKEY_ORIGINS`) so people can use a device instead of a code.
- Settings → Security lists where each person is signed in and ends any session.
- When someone leaves, remove them from the team the same day: their sessions end at once.

## 6. Logs and monitoring

- Server and worker logs leave out email addresses and credentials. Keep that on (it is unless `KEYSTONE_LOG_REDACTION=off`).
- Send logs to a store you control, kept as long as your policy says.
- Set `KEYSTONE_ALERT_EMAIL` so a failing backup or a paused sender reaches someone.
- `DOCUSTAY_TELEMETRY=off` stops the one anonymous daily usage ping (it never carries document content).

## 7. Keep it current

- Upgrade when a release comes out ([upgrade guide](/docs/self-host-upgrade)). Release notes say when a fix is about security.
- Run `docker compose pull` and rebuild at least monthly, so the operating system packages in each image stay patched.
- Report a problem to security@docustay.app.

## 8. Check it

Before the first real document:

1. Open `https://your-address/` and confirm the padlock, then `curl -sI https://your-address/ | grep -i strict-transport` shows HSTS.
2. From outside the host, confirm the database port (5432) and the file store port (8333) do not answer.

```bash
# run from another machine: each line must say "closed" (nc exits non-zero when nothing answers)
for p in 5432 8333 3000; do nc -z -w 3 your-address "$p" && echo "$p OPEN: close it" || echo "$p closed"; done
```

3. With two-step required, sign in as a team member without it: Docustay shows one page with a Set up button.
4. With idle sign-out set, leave a session idle past the limit: the next click asks you to sign in again.
5. Open a document, then check Settings → Security → Access log shows it.
6. Restore last night's backup onto a spare machine and open a signed PDF. Write down how long it took.


---

# Put Docustay behind your own address

The web container listens on port 8080 (change it with `DOCUSTAY_PORT` in `.env`). Everything people use goes through that one port. Put a reverse proxy in front of it to get your own domain and HTTPS.

## Tell Docustay its address

Set the address people will type, with no trailing slash, in `.env`, then restart:

```bash
KEYSTONE_PUBLIC_URL=https://sign.example.com
```

This is the start of every signing link and reset link in an email. If it is wrong, the links in emails will not open.

## Caddy

Caddy gets and renews the certificate for you.

```caddyfile
sign.example.com {
  reverse_proxy localhost:8080
}
```

## nginx

```nginx
server {
  listen 443 ssl http2;
  server_name sign.example.com;
  ssl_certificate     /etc/letsencrypt/live/sign.example.com/fullchain.pem;
  ssl_certificate_key /etc/letsencrypt/live/sign.example.com/privkey.pem;
  client_max_body_size 50m;                        # uploaded documents
  location / {
    proxy_pass http://127.0.0.1:8080;
    proxy_set_header Host $host;
    proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-Proto $scheme;
    proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-For $remote_addr;
  }
}
```

## Traefik (labels on the web service)

```yaml
services:
  web:
    labels:
      - traefik.enable=true
      - traefik.http.routers.docustay.rule=Host(`sign.example.com`)
      - traefik.http.routers.docustay.tls.certresolver=letsencrypt
      - traefik.http.services.docustay.loadbalancer.server.port=3000
```

## Check

- Open `https://sign.example.com/login`. The sign-in page should load over HTTPS with no certificate warning.
- Send yourself a document and open the link in the email. It must start with your address.
- If you use embedded signing, list your own website under Settings → Developers → Embedding.

## Keep the proxy honest

Pass `X-Forwarded-Proto` and `X-Forwarded-For` as shown, **and add `DOCUSTAY_CLIENT_IP_HEADER=X-Forwarded-For` to `.env`** (then `docker compose up -d`). Docustay uses the first to know a request was secure and the second for the address in the audit trail, on the signing certificate and in the rate limits; without the setting it can only see the proxy's own address. Set it only when a proxy you control is in front (otherwise anyone could write their own address into the header); `DOCUSTAY_PROXY_COUNT` is how many proxies there are (default 1). Do not expose ports 5432 (database), 8333 (file store) or 3000 (web) directly.

## Public form links

Forms need nothing extra on your own servers. A published form is served at `/f/<workspace>/<link name>` by the same web container as the rest of the app, and the people who fill it in never sign in. Two things to keep in mind at the proxy: pass `/f/` through like any other path, and do not add your own `X-Frame-Options` or `frame-ancestors` header, because Docustay sets `frame-ancestors` itself (only the websites listed on a form may show it in a frame; with none listed, nobody can).


---

# Pro licence keys

Community is free under the AGPL-3.0 and needs no key. Pro is a yearly licence for your own business, and it unlocks the Pro features on your install. This page follows a key from purchase to renewal.

## 1. Buy

Choose Self-host Pro on the [Self-host](/self-host) page and pay by card. When the payment is confirmed, a key is made for you and emailed once to the address on the payment. We keep only a fingerprint of the key, never the key itself, so it cannot be shown again. Keep the email.

## 2. Install the key

Add it to the `.env` of your install and restart:

```bash
DOCUSTAY_LICENSE_KEY=<the key from the email>
```

```bash
docker compose up -d
```

The first time the app starts with a key it has not used before, it downloads the Pro add-on from docustay.app. Your key and the install's own id are sent; a key that is valid, not ended and not cancelled, and that belongs to this install, gets the add-on (a different install gets the same refusal as a wrong key). The add-on is checked against its digest before it is unpacked into the install's data folder. To fetch it again or after a failure:

```bash
docker compose exec app node docustay/selfhost/addon.mjs pull
docker compose restart app worker
```

The install then checks the key against the public key shipped with it (`license-public.pem`). That check happens on your machine: a key is valid if it was signed by us, has not ended, and was not cancelled.

## 3. Renewal

When your yearly payment succeeds, the key is extended to the end of the paid year plus 14 days of grace, so a late card does not switch your install off. You do not need to change anything: an install that can reach docustay.app renews its record by itself.

## 4. Working offline

An install with no route to the internet cannot renew by itself. Open Settings and download the usage report (it holds five whole numbers and an install id, never a document, name or address), and send it to us when we ask. You can also turn off the daily anonymous ping with `DOCUSTAY_TELEMETRY=off`; the key still works.

## 5. When the licence ends

If you cancel or the grace days pass, the Pro features stop (the add-on stays in the data folder but is not loaded without a live licence). Your documents, signed PDFs and settings are not touched, and the install keeps running as Community. Nothing is deleted.

## Lost key?

Write to the address on your payment receipt.


---

# Tutorial: e-signatures in a Next.js app

You will end up with three small files: a route that sends a document, a page that shows the signing form, and a route that checks Docustay's webhook. The finished app is in `docustay/examples/nextjs`. It takes about ten minutes.

## 1. What you need

- A Docustay account and a **test** API key (Developers). A test key sends nothing real and bills nothing.
- A template. Make one in the app (Templates → Create) and copy its id from the address bar.
- Your site's address listed under Settings → Developers → Embedding (`http://localhost:3000` while you try it).

## 2. Install

```bash
npm install @docustay2026/sdk @docustay2026/embed
```

Put the secrets in `.env.local`. They stay on the server:

```bash
DOCUSTAY_API_KEY=dsk_test_…
DOCUSTAY_TEMPLATE_ID=<template id>
DOCUSTAY_WEBHOOK_SECRET=whsec_…
```

## 3. Send a document

`app/api/send/route.js` turns a name and an email into a document whose signer signs in your page, so nobody is emailed:

```js
import { Docustay } from "@docustay2026/sdk";

export async function POST(req) {
  const { name, email } = await req.json();
  const docustay = new Docustay(process.env.DOCUSTAY_API_KEY);
  const doc = await docustay.sendDocument({
    templateId: process.env.DOCUSTAY_TEMPLATE_ID,
    embedded: ["signer_1"],
    parties: [{ seat: "signer_1", name, email }],
  });
  return Response.json({ id: doc.id });
}
```

## 4. Show the signing form

A server component asks for a link that lasts one hour. It is made on the server, so the key never reaches the browser:

```js
const { url } = await docustay.embedSession(id, { seat: "signer_1", origin: "http://localhost:3000" });
```

A small client component then renders `<docustay-sign url={url} height="720" />` and listens for the `completed` event. See `app/sign` in the example.

## 5. Check the webhook

Docustay signs every webhook. Read the body as text and verify it before you trust it:

```js
import { verifyWebhook } from "@docustay2026/sdk";

export async function POST(req) {
  try {
    const event = await verifyWebhook(process.env.DOCUSTAY_WEBHOOK_SECRET, req.headers, await req.text());
    // event.topic is for example documents.document.executed, event.subject_id is the document
    return new Response(null, { status: 204 });
  } catch { return new Response("bad signature", { status: 400 }); }
}
```

On your laptop, run `npx docustay listen --forward-to http://localhost:3000/api/webhooks`. It prints the secret to use and forwards real, signed events to your route.

## 6. Try it

```bash
curl -X POST localhost:3000/api/send -H 'content-type: application/json' -d '{"name":"Pat Example","email":"pat@example.com"}'
```

Open `/sign?id=<the id it returns>`, sign, and watch your webhook route log `documents.document.executed`. When it works, swap in a live key.


---

# Tutorial: send a document from Python

This tutorial uses the Python SDK and nothing else, so it runs on any machine with Python 3. The finished program is `docustay/examples/python/app.py`.

## 1. What you need

A Docustay **test** API key, a template id, and Python 3.9 or newer.

```bash
pip install docustay
export DOCUSTAY_API_KEY=dsk_test_…
export DOCUSTAY_TEMPLATE_ID=<template id>
```

## 2. Send one document

```python
import os
from docustay import Docustay

docustay = Docustay(os.environ["DOCUSTAY_API_KEY"])
doc = docustay.send_document(
    os.environ["DOCUSTAY_TEMPLATE_ID"],
    [{"seat": "signer_1", "name": "Pat Example", "email": "pat@example.com"}],
)
print(doc["id"], doc["state"])
```

With a test key, Pat is not emailed; the document is made so you can try the whole flow. To see it as the signer, call `docustay.test_sign(doc["id"], "signer_1")`.

## 3. Wait for the result with a webhook

Polling works but a webhook is better. Docustay signs each delivery; `verify_webhook` refuses a changed body, a wrong secret and an old timestamp:

```python
from docustay import verify_webhook

event = verify_webhook(secret, headers, raw_body)   # raw_body is the exact text received
if event["topic"] == "documents.document.executed":
    print("signed:", event["subject_id"])
```

Use the raw body. If you parse the JSON first and serialise it again, the signature will not match.

On your laptop, `npx docustay listen --forward-to http://localhost:3000/webhooks` forwards real signed events and prints the secret.

## 4. Download the signed copy

```python
open("signed.pdf", "wb").write(docustay.download_signed_pdf(doc["id"]))
```

## 5. Errors and limits

Every failure raises `DocustayError` with the HTTP status and the message from Docustay. Network failures and `429` answers are retried for you. Pass `idempotency_key=` to a send if you might call it twice for the same event; the second call returns the first result instead of sending again.

## 6. Go further

The whole example, with the page that embeds the signing form, is `docustay/examples/python/app.py`. Swap in a live key only once the test flow works.


---

# Tutorial: let an AI agent draft contracts, with a person approving

An agent is good at drafting and bad at knowing when a document should leave the building. Docustay lets you give it the first and keep the second. This takes about ten minutes.

## 1. Make the agent its own key

In Developers, make a key named for the agent:

- Environment: **test** while you try it.
- Scopes: `documents:read`, `documents:write`, `templates:read`. Nothing else.
- Tick **Draft only**.
- Optionally set **drafts per day** and **sends per day**. They are exact, and past the limit the key gets a `429`.

Give the agent that key and nothing more.

## 2. What the agent can do

The agent creates a draft from a template or from text, checks it, and edits it:

```js
const draft = await docustay.createDocument({ title: "Services agreement", source, people });
const check = await docustay.checkDocument({ source, people });   // read every problem it lists
```

It can ask to send:

```js
const r = await docustay.sendDraft(draft.id);   // answers 202, state "draft", approval.status "pending"
```

Nothing is emailed. The document stays a draft, and asking again returns the same request, not a second one.

## 3. A person approves

Open Settings → Developers → Approvals. Each waiting request shows the document, the key that asked, and when. Open the document, read it, then press **Approve and send** or **Decline**. Approving sends it now, as you. Declining leaves it a draft for the agent or a person to change.

## 4. See what the agent did

On the same screen, **What your keys did** lists every call the key made (route and answer, never the contents of the request, so a prompt never lands in the log) and every request with who decided it.

## 5. Tell the agent the rules

Add the published skill to your agent so it behaves: `docustay-agent-safety` in the Docustay Claude plugin (`sdk/claude-plugin`). It tells the agent to use a test key first, to read every problem a check reports, to stop on a `429`, and to tell you when a send is waiting instead of retrying.

## 6. Going live

When the test flow works, make a live draft-only key with limits that suit you. Keep **Draft only** on until you trust the agent's drafts; turning it off is a change you make to that key, not something the agent can do.


---

# Single sign-on with OpenID Connect

A self-hosted install can offer **Sign in with your identity provider** next to the password form. It uses the standard OpenID Connect authorization-code flow with PKCE, so it works with any provider that follows the standard.

## What it does and does not do

- It is another way **in** for people who already have an account on this install. It never creates one: someone your provider vouches for, but who has no Docustay account here, is refused. Invite them first.
- It matches by email address, and only when the provider says the address is verified (`email_verified` is true).
- Two-step sign-in rules are unchanged. It only replaces the password step.
- Passwords keep working. Turning single sign-on on does not lock anyone out.

## Set it up

1. At your provider, make a client for Docustay. The sign-in redirect address is your address plus `/api/auth/oidc/callback`, for example `https://sign.example.com/api/auth/oidc/callback`.
2. Put these in `.env` next to the other settings, then recreate the containers:

```bash
DOCUSTAY_OIDC_ISSUER=https://sso.example.com/realms/main
DOCUSTAY_OIDC_CLIENT_ID=docustay
DOCUSTAY_OIDC_CLIENT_SECRET=<the client secret>
DOCUSTAY_OIDC_LABEL=Example SSO
```

```bash
docker compose up -d --force-recreate app worker web
```

3. Open the sign-in page. A button named after your label appears. The address you set in `KEYSTONE_PUBLIC_URL` must be the one people use, because the provider sends them back to it.

## If it does not work

- Look at the app's log: `docker compose logs app`. Lines that start `oidc:` say why a sign-in was refused, without any secret.
- "No email in the token": your provider keeps the email in its userinfo answer. Docustay asks for it there; make sure the scopes include `email`.
- "The provider does not vouch for the email": turn on email verification at your provider.


---

# Search, contracts, payments and automations

These calls do what the app's own screens do: the search box, the Contracts view of Documents, the Payments tab of Billing and the Automations canvas. Each one calls the same code as the screen, so the API and the app always give the same answer.

| You want to | Call | Scope |
|---|---|---|
| Find documents, templates, forms and people | `GET /api/v1/search?q=…` | `documents:read` |
| List signed contracts with their key dates | `GET /api/v1/contracts` | `documents:read` |
| Correct one key date by hand | `POST /api/v1/contracts/{id}/dates` | `documents:write` |
| List payments taken while signing | `GET /api/v1/payments` | `documents:read` |
| Refund a payment, in full or in part | `POST /api/v1/payments/{id}/refund` | `documents:write` |
| List the automations built on the canvas | `GET /api/v1/automations` | `plays:read` |
| Switch an automation on or off | `POST /api/v1/automations/{id}/enable` | `plays:write` |

A key without the scope gets `401`, the same answer as a wrong key. Another workspace's document, payment or automation is `404`: a key never learns that it exists.

## Search

`q` is the words to look for. `per` is how many of each kind come back (1 to 20, default 6). The answer is grouped into `documents`, `templates` (forms are in here too, with `kind: "form"`) and `people`, best match first.

```js
const r = await docustay.search("Deposit", { per: 5 });
for (const d of r.groups.documents) console.log(d.id, d.state, d.title);
```

## Contracts and key dates

When a document is signed, Docustay reads its start, end, notice and renewal dates and its value from the boxes the signers filled in. `GET /api/v1/contracts` lists every signed document with those dates. Each date says where it came from in `source`: a box on the document, or a person's correction. `q` filters by title, person or amount. The `summary` counts every signed contract, and the ones with a renewal, end or notice date in the next 30 days.

A date read wrongly can be corrected. The signed PDF never changes. The correction is kept as the person's, and renewal reminders follow it. Send `date: null` to clear one.

```js
await docustay.setContractDate(contractId, { kind: "end", date: "2027-01-31" });
```

## Payments

A payment box on a document takes the money while the person signs. `GET /api/v1/payments` lists them newest first, with this month's figures in `month`. Each payment has its `status`:

| Status | Means |
|---|---|
| `paid` | Stripe took the money |
| `waiting` | signed, and the signature is kept while they pay (for up to 7 days) |
| `started` | they opened the payment and did not finish it |
| `refunded` / `partially_refunded` | some or all of it was given back |
| `disputed` | the payer's bank opened a dispute; answer it in Stripe |

In `month`, `stripeFee` is Stripe's own fees on this month's payments, and `stripeFeePending` counts the payments Stripe has not settled yet (that can take a few minutes). Page through with `before`, using `next` from the previous page.

### Refunds

A refund goes through Stripe on your workspace's own Stripe account. Leave out `amountMinor` to refund the rest of the payment, or give it in the smallest unit of the currency (`500` is 5.00). `reason` is required: the payer sees it on their receipt, and it goes in the document's audit trail. The signed document stays signed.

A refund moves money, so it needs an `Idempotency-Key`. Send the same key again and you get the first answer back, with no second refund. The SDKs add a key for you and reuse it when they retry.

```js
const r = await docustay.refundPayment(paymentId, { amountMinor: 500, reason: "Charged twice" });
console.log(r.status, r.refundedLabel);   // "partially_refunded", "$5.00"
```

```python
docustay.refund_payment(payment_id, reason="Charged twice")   # the rest of the payment
```

From the command line, `docustay payments refund <id> --reason "…" --yes` does the same. It never runs without `--yes`, or a typed yes at the prompt.

## Automations

An automation built on the canvas starts when a document from a chosen template or form is signed, then runs its steps: wait, check an answer, send the next document. `GET /api/v1/automations` lists them with whether each is on, how many times it ran and when it last ran. (`GET /api/v1/playbooks` lists playbooks: packs of templates and skills. See [the template library](/docs/template-library.md).)

`POST /api/v1/automations/{id}/enable` with `{ "on": true }` switches one on, which needs Pro. From then on, each matching signed document starts a run. `{ "on": false }` stops new runs. A run that is already waiting stops when its wait ends, without sending anything.

```js
await docustay.setAutomationOn(automationId, true);
```

## From an AI assistant

The MCP server has `search_documents`, `list_contracts`, `set_contract_date`, `list_payments` and `list_automations`. It has no tool to refund a payment or to switch an automation on: those move money or start sending documents to people, so a person does them in the app, from the command line or from their own code.


---

# The template library

Every workspace has 54 built-in templates beside its own: 24 **Document templates** (sent to the people you name) and 30 **Form templates** (one link many people fill in). They are on the Templates page in two tabs, and the same list is on the API, the SDKs, the CLI and the MCP server.

A built-in is a **read-only master**. There are two ways to use one:

- **Send straight from it.** A draft is made from the built-in with no copy, so it does **not** count toward Free's 5 new templates a month. The document counts toward the month's documents when it is sent, like any other. A Form template is published as it is.
- **Customize it.** You get your own editable copy. That is a new template, so it counts toward the monthly limit on Free (Pro and self-hosted installs have none). On a workspace that asks for approval, a member's copy waits for an owner or admin.

A new version of a template never counts. A built-in can never be edited, renamed, retired or replaced by hand: ask for a copy instead.

| You want to | Call | Scope |
|---|---|---|
| List the built-in templates | `GET /api/v1/templates/library?kind=document` or `form` | `templates:read` |
| One built-in with its fields and guidance | `GET /api/v1/templates/library/{slug}` | `templates:read` |
| A draft from a built-in | `POST /api/v1/templates/library/{slug}/documents` | `templates:write` |
| Your own copy of a built-in | `POST /api/v1/templates/library/{slug}/customize` | `templates:write` |
| Start a draft that asks the template's own questions | `POST /api/v1/drafts` with `{ "template": "services-agreement", "people": [...] }` | `drafts:write` |

`documents:read` and `documents:write` open the same routes.

```js
const { templates } = await docustay.listLibraryTemplates({ kind: "document" });
const draft = await docustay.draftFromLibraryTemplate("mutual-nda");   // not a new template
const mine = await docustay.customizeLibraryTemplate("mutual-nda", { name: "Our NDA" }); // a new template
```

From the command line: `docustay templates library --kind form` and `docustay templates customize mutual-nda`. The MCP server has `list_library_templates`, `get_library_template` and `draft_from_library_template`.

## Skills, playbooks and automations

- A **skill** (the Plays page; `/api/v1/plays`) guides how a document is written: a built-in add-on such as a late fee, a house style such as Plain English, or your own (Pro). A skill never picks a template. Each template carries its own questions, facts and checklist as guidance, which Scribe reads after it finds the template.
- A **playbook** (`/api/v1/playbooks`) is a pack of templates and skills for one job, such as a new-tenant pack. Switching one on puts its templates first on the Templates page and for Scribe. The built-in packs are free to switch on; making your own is Pro. `POST /api/v1/playbooks/{name}/enable` with `{ "enabled": true }` switches one.
- An **automation** (`/api/v1/automations`) runs on its own when a document is signed: wait, check an answer, send the next document. A send step can pick any template in the library. See [Search, contracts, payments and automations](/docs/contracts-payments-playbooks.md).

## Draft from a template with its own questions

`POST /api/v1/drafts` (part of Docustay Pro; a Free workspace gets a 403 that says so) starts from a built-in Document template and asks that template's questions first (up to four at a time, each with two to four options). Answer them with `POST /api/v1/drafts/{draftRef}/answers`. Nothing is ever sent: a draft is a draft.

```bash
curl -X POST https://app.docustay.app/api/v1/drafts \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $DOCUSTAY_KEY" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{ "template": "services-agreement", "people": [{ "name": "Ana Client", "email": "ana@example.com", "role": "Client" }] }'
```

A Form template is published, not drafted for named people: use `POST /api/v1/forms/publish` with the template's id from the library list.

## Settings → Templates

An owner or admin can ask that a member's templates wait for approval (on by default) and can hide the built-in library. Hiding it removes the built-in tabs and refuses new use and customizing; a built-in that a form or an automation already uses keeps working. Self-hosted installs print every built-in on install and bring them up to date on upgrade.
